input:
It should be emphasised that the contingency allowance for the upgrade project is currently set at 11%, and there are several important reasons why this figure should be maintained rather than reduced at this stage. Essentially, the figures presented in the cost table in the Costs section relate only to the defined scope of the project. The allowance, by contrast, is intended to cover an entirely different category of cost: namely, items that the project will certainly require but which cannot yet be defined with sufficient precision to be priced individually. Between the current estimate and FID, items progressively move from the second category into the first as the design work defines them more clearly, and the history of that movement, as reflected in the estimate's own revisions, provides the most reliable measure of the allowance that the project actually needs.

A lower allowance would effectively assume that the undefined scope is smaller than the current position genuinely supports. The undefined items are not optional extras that can simply be removed; rather, they represent work whose absence from the priced list merely reflects the present stage of design, and not any judgement that the work itself will not ultimately be carried out. Reducing the allowance does not reduce that work in any way. Instead, it simply converts an explicit provision into an overrun that will only emerge after approval has been given, at a point when the steering group will have far fewer options available for absorbing it.

The allowance is held against the undefined items as a class, and it is drawn upon only as items become defined and are priced into the base estimate. On this basis, 11% is the figure that the estimate supports at the present stage: it corresponds to the share of cost that remains undefined, and it naturally falls as definition proceeds, since each defined item transfers its cost from the allowance into the priced table. The steering group reviews the balance at every revision of the cost table, and the allowance that the project eventually carries into FID is the residue remaining after those transfers, rather than the figure that is being defended here.
